sections.title: Document Structure & Metadata
sections.description: Understand DOCTYPE, character encoding, viewport directives, and how browsers parse HTML into the DOM.

lessons.title: HTML5 Document Boilerplate & DOCTYPE
lessons.summary: Every modern HTML document starts with <!DOCTYPE html>, which triggers standards-compliant rendering mode instead of legacy quirks mode.
explanation: Every modern HTML document starts with <!DOCTYPE html>, which triggers standards-compliant rendering mode instead of legacy quirks mode.

The root <html> element declares the document language via lang="en", allowing screen readers to select the right pronunciation voice and search engines to index regional content accurately. Inside <head>, metadata configures parsing before body paint.
Place <meta charset="UTF-8"> as the very first element inside <head> so the browser determines encoding within the first 1024 bytes.

codeExample.title: Minimal Standards-Mode HTML5 Document
codeExample.code: Welcome
codeExample.output: Renders in Standards Mode with UTF-8 decoding and mobile-responsive viewport scaling.

keyPoints: <!DOCTYPE html> is case-insensitive and prevents browser quirks mode.
Always set the lang attribute on <html> for screen readers and translation tools.
The viewport meta tag ensures CSS pixels match device-independent pixels on mobile.

commonMistakes.mistake: Omitting <!DOCTYPE html> in legacy templates
commonMistakes.fix: Always place <!DOCTYPE html> on line 1 with zero preceding whitespace or comments.

commonMistakes.mistake: Disabling zoom with user-scalable=no
commonMistakes.fix: Keep zoom enabled (width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0) to satisfy WCAG accessibility guidelines.

interviewQA.question: What happens if you omit <!DOCTYPE html>?
interviewQA.answer: Browsers fall back to quirks mode, altering box-model sizing, table inheritance, and font scaling for backward compatibility with 1990s pages.

interviewQA.question: Why does <meta charset="UTF-8"> belong near the top of <head>?
interviewQA.answer: HTML parsers scan the first 1024 bytes for encoding; placing it early prevents reparsing and mojibake characters.

lessons.title: Head Metadata, Favicons & Resource Hints
lessons.summary: The <head> element holds machine-readable metadata, stylesheets, icons, and network hints that shape loading speed and social previews.
explanation: The <head> element holds machine-readable metadata, stylesheets, icons, and network hints that shape loading speed and social previews.

Using <link rel="preconnect"> warms up DNS, TCP, and TLS handshakes for critical third-party origins such as font CDNs, while <meta name="description"> supplies concise summaries for search result snippets.
Defer non-critical scripts with defer so HTML parsing is never blocked during initial render.

codeExample.title: Head Configuration with Preconnect & Deferred Script
codeExample.code:
<head>
  <meta charset="UTF-8" />
  <title>API Docs — IT Courses</title>
  <meta name="description" content="Complete REST and GraphQL reference." />
  <link rel="preconnect" href="https://fonts.googleapis.com" />
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="/styles/app.css" />
  <script src="/scripts/app.js" defer></script>
</head>

keyPoints: defer downloads scripts in parallel and executes them in document order after HTML parsing completes.
async executes immediately upon download, which can break script dependency order.
Avoid placing visible content elements inside <head>; parsers will prematurely close <head>.

commonMistakes.mistake: Putting blocking <script> tags in <head> without defer or async
commonMistakes.fix: Add defer (or type="module", which defers by default) so parsing continues uninterrupted.

commonMistakes.mistake: Duplicate <title> elements or missing descriptions
commonMistakes.fix: Provide one unique, descriptive <title> per route for tabs, bookmarks, and screen readers.

interviewQA.question: How do defer and async differ on <script> tags?
interviewQA.answer: Both download asynchronously without blocking HTML parsing, but defer preserves execution order and runs right before DOMContentLoaded, whereas async executes as soon as download finishes in arbitrary order.

interviewQA.question: When should you use preconnect vs dns-prefetch?
interviewQA.answer: Use preconnect for critical origins needed immediately (it completes DNS + TCP + TLS); use dns-prefetch as a lightweight fallback for lower-priority domains.

lessons.title: HTML Parsing, Entities & Whitespace Collapsing
lessons.summary: Browsers collapse consecutive spaces, tabs, and newlines in normal flow into a single space while decoding named and numeric character references.
explanation: Browsers collapse consecutive spaces, tabs, and newlines in normal flow into a single space while decoding named and numeric character references.
Reserved syntax characters like <, >, and & must be escaped as <, >, and & when displayed literally inside prose or <code> blocks to prevent accidental tag parsing or XSS injection.
Use semantic elements like <pre> and <code> when preserving indentation instead of chaining   entities.

keyPoints: HTML collapses runs of ASCII whitespace into a single space outside <pre> or CSS white-space: pre.
Escape <, >, &, and quotes inside attributes to prevent malformed DOM trees.
UTF-8 eliminates the need for most named entities beyond reserved syntax characters.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using multiple   entities for layout spacing
commonMistakes.fix: Use CSS margin, padding, or gap utilities instead of non-breaking space characters.

commonMistakes.mistake: Writing unescaped < or > inside <code> examples
commonMistakes.fix: Always encode < as < and > as > so the browser renders text rather than parsing an HTML tag.

interviewQA.question: Why must & be escaped as & in HTML text and URLs?
interviewQA.answer: An unescaped & signals the start of a character entity reference, which can corrupt query strings like ?a=1&copy=2 into ©=2.

interviewQA.question:

sections.title: Semantic Landmarks & Headings
sections.description: Replace generic div soup with meaningful landmarks that power navigation, reader mode, and assistive technology.

lessons.title: Page Landmarks: header, nav, main, aside, footer
lessons.summary: Landmark elements expose the macro layout of a page directly to the browser accessibility tree.
explanation: Landmark elements expose the macro layout of a page directly to the browser accessibility tree.

Screen reader users jump directly between landmarks like <main> and <nav> instead of tabbing through dozens of links. Only one visible <main> element should exist per page, and multiple <nav> regions should be distinguished with aria-label.
Avoid wrapping every card in <section> unless it has its own heading; use <div> for purely stylistic layout wrappers.

codeExample.title: Semantic Page Landmark Skeleton
codeExample.code:
IT Courses
Courses Practice

Semantic HTML

© 2026 IT Courses

keyPoints: Every page should have a single primary <main> landmark.
Label multiple <nav> elements with aria-label (e.g. "Primary", "Breadcrumb").
<header> and <footer> can also be scoped inside <article> or <section>.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using <div class="header"> and <div class="main"> everywhere
commonMistakes.fix: Use native <header>, <nav>, <main>, and <footer> landmarks for built-in accessibility roles.

commonMistakes.mistake: Placing <main> inside <header> or <article>
commonMistakes.fix: Keep <main> as a top-level landmark unique to the document content.

interviewQA.question: When should you use <article> vs <section>?
interviewQA.answer: Use <article> for self-contained content that still makes sense syndicated on its own (blog post, product card); use <section> to group thematically related content with a heading.

interviewQA.question: Why is labeling multiple <nav> landmarks important?
interviewQA.answer: Assistive technology lists all navigation landmarks; without distinct aria-label names, users hear "navigation" repeated without context.

lessons.title: Heading Hierarchy (h1–h6) & Document Outline
lessons.summary: Headings create a navigable table of contents for both human scanners and assistive technology users.
explanation: Headings create a navigable table of contents for both human scanners and assistive technology users.

Start every page with one clear <h1> describing the primary view, then nest <h2>, <h3>, and <h4> sequentially without skipping levels purely for font size. Style visual size with CSS classes rather than choosing <h4> because it looks smaller.
Check your heading outline during code review: every section heading should nest logically under its parent topic.

codeExample.title: Proper Sequential Heading Hierarchy
codeExample.code:
PostgreSQL Indexing Guide

B-Tree Indexes

Composite Key Ordering

GIN Indexes

keyPoints: Never skip heading levels (e.g., jumping from <h1> straight to <h4>) just to shrink text.
Decouple heading semantics (h1–h6) from visual font size using CSS.
Screen reader users rely on heading shortcuts (H key) as their #1 navigation method.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using <h1> for the small navbar logo on every page
commonMistakes.fix: Use <a> or <span> for the navbar brand and reserve <h1> for the unique main heading of the page.

commonMistakes.mistake:
Using bold

tags instead of

for section titles
commonMistakes.fix: Use true heading elements so document outlines and anchor links work properly.

interviewQA.question: Is having multiple <h1> elements allowed in HTML5?
interviewQA.answer: Although early specs proposed an outline algorithm for nested <h1>s, browsers never implemented it; best practice for accessibility and SEO is one <h1> per page with sequential h2–h6 levels.

interviewQA.question: How do you make an <h2> look smaller without breaking semantics?
interviewQA.answer: Keep the tag as <h2> and apply a smaller CSS font-size utility class.

lessons.title: Inline Text Semantics: strong, em, time, abbr, mark
lessons.summary: Inline semantic tags communicate emphasis, machine-readable dates, abbreviations, and highlighted matches beyond raw styling.
explanation: Inline semantic tags communicate emphasis, machine-readable dates, abbreviations, and highlighted matches beyond raw styling.

<strong> conveys strong importance while <em> conveys vocal stress emphasis—unlike purely stylistic <b> and <i>. The <time datetime="..."> element lets crawlers and calendar tools parse ISO timestamps reliably.
Pair <time> with an ISO 8601 datetime attribute so human-friendly text like "Nov 18" remains machine-readable.

codeExample.title: Rich Inline Text Semantics
codeExample.code: Published on November 18, 2026. Warning: Always escape HTML in untrusted user input.

keyPoints: <strong> marks high importance; <em> marks stress emphasis that changes sentence meaning.
<time datetime="YYYY-MM-DD"> bridges human readability and machine parsing.
<mark> highlights search query matches or relevant reference passages.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using <b> and <i> for warnings or key terms
commonMistakes.fix: Use <strong> for critical warnings and <em> for emphasis; reserve <b>/<i> for stylistic offset only.

commonMistakes.mistake: Writing human text inside datetime="Nov 18"
commonMistakes.fix: Always use valid ISO 8601 format like datetime="2026-11-18" in the datetime attribute.

interviewQA.question: What is the semantic difference between <strong> and <b>?
interviewQA.answer: <strong> indicates importance or urgency (conveyed semantically), while <b> merely draws visual attention (like keywords in a summary) without extra importance.

interviewQA.question: When is <mark> preferred over <strong>?
interviewQA.answer: Use <mark> when highlighting text relevant to the user’s current context (such as search matches), not intrinsic authorial importance.

lessons.title: Figures, Quotations & Code Annotations
lessons.summary: Use <figure>, <figcaption>, <blockquote>, <cite>, <kbd>, and <samp> to annotate technical documentation cleanly.
explanation: Use <figure>, <figcaption>, <blockquote>, <cite>, <kbd>, and <samp> to annotate technical documentation cleanly.
<figure> associates self-contained diagrams, code listings, or charts with a descriptive <figcaption>. For technical tutorials, <kbd> denotes keyboard input and <samp> denotes program output.
Place the cite attribute on <blockquote> for machine-readable source URLs and wrap visible work titles in <cite>.

codeExample.title: Technical Documentation Figure & Quotation
codeExample.code: Semantic markup improves interoperability across devices.

keyPoints: <figure> is not limited to images—it can wrap code blocks, tables, or SVG charts.
<figcaption> must be the first or last child inside <figure>.
<kbd> represents user keyboard input; <samp> represents system output.

commonMistakes.mistake: Putting <figcaption> outside <figure>
commonMistakes.fix: Always place <figcaption> directly inside <figure> as its first or last child.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using <blockquote> just to indent text visually
commonMistakes.fix: Use CSS padding/margin for indentation; reserve <blockquote> strictly for quoted external content.

interviewQA.question: Can a <figure> contain a code snippet or table?
interviewQA.answer: Yes. Any self-contained content referenced from the main flow—diagrams, code blocks, quotes, or tables—belongs in <figure>.

interviewQA.question: What does <kbd> signify in HTML?
interviewQA.answer: It represents user input such as keyboard shortcuts, voice commands, or terminal keystrokes.

sections.title: Links, Navigation & Lists
sections.description: Master relative vs root-relative URLs, secure external links, download links, and structured list types.

lessons.title: Hyperlinks, Target Security & Fragment Navigation
lessons.summary: Anchor elements connect documents, jump to in-page IDs, initiate downloads, and trigger mailto or tel schemes.
explanation: Anchor elements connect documents, jump to in-page IDs, initiate downloads, and trigger mailto or tel schemes.

Opening external links in a new tab with target="_blank" should include rel="noopener noreferrer" (modern browsers default to noopener, but explicit attributes protect older environments and control referrer leakage).
Write descriptive link text ("Read the PostgreSQL syllabus") instead of generic "Click here" so screen reader link lists make sense out of context.

codeExample.title: Secure External Links & In-Page Anchors
codeExample.code: Jump to syllabus MDN HTML Reference Download PDF Cheatsheet

keyPoints: rel="noopener" prevents the opened tab from accessing window.opener (reverse tabnabbing).
The download attribute only works cleanly for same-origin URLs or blob/data URLs.
Fragment links (#section-id) scroll to and focus the element with matching id.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using <span onclick="..."> for page navigation
commonMistakes.fix: Always use <a href="..."> so right-click, open-in-new-tab, and keyboard Enter work natively.

commonMistakes.mistake: Writing "Click here" or "Read more" for every link
commonMistakes.fix: Include the link destination in the anchor text for accessibility and SEO clarity.

interviewQA.question: Why is rel="noopener" paired with target="_blank"?
interviewQA.answer: It severs the window.opener reference so an external page cannot redirect the originating tab to a phishing page.

interviewQA.question: When is the download attribute ignored by browsers?
interviewQA.answer: When pointing to a cross-origin resource without matching Content-Disposition headers, browsers navigate instead of forcing a download for security.

lessons.title: Ordered, Unordered & Description Lists
lessons.summary: HTML provides three list types: <ul> for unordered collections, <ol> for sequential steps, and <dl> for key-value term definitions.
explanation: HTML provides three list types: <ul> for unordered collections, <ol> for sequential steps, and <dl> for key-value term definitions.
Description lists (<dl> with <dt> terms and <dd> definitions) are ideal for glossaries, metadata specs, and FAQ pairs. Ordered lists support start, reversed, and type attributes for custom numbering.
Only <li> elements are valid direct children of <ul> and <ol>; place nested lists inside an <li>, never directly inside the parent <ul>.

codeExample.title: Ordered Steps & Key-Value Description List
codeExample.code:
1. Deploy build
  2. Run tests
  3. Write code
HTTP 201
Resource created successfully.
HTTP 409
Conflict with current server state.
codeExample.output: 3. Deploy build  2. Run tests  1. Write code

keyPoints: Use <ol> when sequence order changes meaning (steps, rankings); use <ul> otherwise.
<dl> pairs one or more <dt> terms with one or more <dd> descriptions.
Nested lists must live inside an <li> of the outer list.

commonMistakes.mistake: Placing a <ul> directly inside another <ul> instead of inside an <li>
commonMistakes.fix: Close nested lists inside the parent <li> before starting the next <li>.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using <div> stacks for glossary key-value pairs
commonMistakes.fix: Use <dl>, <dt>, and <dd> to convey term-definition relationships semantically.

interviewQA.question: What direct child elements are allowed inside <ul> and <ol>?
interviewQA.answer: Strictly <li> (and script-supporting elements like <template>); headings or nested lists must sit inside an <li>.

interviewQA.question: Can a single <dt> have multiple <dd> descriptions?
interviewQA.answer: Yes, HTML allows multiple <dt> terms to share a <dd>, or one <dt> to have multiple <dd> values.

lessons.title: Breadcrumb & Skip Navigation Patterns
lessons.summary: Accessible navigation includes a visually hidden skip link at the top of <body> and structured breadcrumb trails on nested pages.
explanation: Accessible navigation includes a visually hidden skip link at the top of <body> and structured breadcrumb trails on nested pages.

A skip link lets keyboard-only users bypass repeated header links on every page load and land directly on <main id="main-content">. Breadcrumbs use <nav aria-label="Breadcrumb"> with an <ol> and aria-current="page" on the final item.
Always apply aria-current="page" to the active navigation link so screen readers announce the user’s current location.

codeExample.title: Skip Link & Accessible Breadcrumb Trail
codeExample.code:
Skip to main content
  1. Home
  2. Courses
  3. HTML

keyPoints: Skip links are the first focusable element inside <body> and become visible on :focus.
Breadcrumbs use <ol> because hierarchy order matters.
aria-current="page" announces the current route in nav bars and breadcrumbs.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using display: none on skip links
commonMistakes.fix: Use visually-hidden (sr-only) CSS that reveals on :focus; display: none removes the link from Tab order completely.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using <ul> instead of <ol> for breadcrumbs
commonMistakes.fix: Use <ol> to reflect the ordered parent-to-child path.

interviewQA.question: What does aria-current="page" communicate?
interviewQA.answer: It tells assistive technology which link inside a set represents the currently displayed page.

interviewQA.question: Why shouldn’t skip links use display: none?
interviewQA.answer: Elements with display: none are non-focusable and excluded from the accessibility tree, making them unreachable by keyboard.

lessons.title: Relative Paths, Base URLs & Fragment IDs
lessons.summary: Understanding relative (./, ../), root-relative (/courses), and absolute URLs prevents broken assets across nested routes.
explanation: Understanding relative (./, ../), root-relative (/courses), and absolute URLs prevents broken assets across nested routes.

In Single Page Applications with nested routes like /courses/html/lesson/1, a relative path like images/logo.png resolves relative to /courses/html/lesson/ and breaks; root-relative /images/logo.png always resolves from the domain root.
Use root-relative paths for shared assets and avoid <base href> unless you fully understand its effect on in-page #fragment links.

codeExample.title: URL Resolution Patterns
codeExample.code: Next Parent Index

keyPoints: Root-relative paths start with / and resolve against the site origin.
Relative paths without a leading slash resolve against the current document URL directory.
Element IDs must be unique within a document and cannot contain whitespace.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using relative asset paths (assets/img.png) inside nested SPA routes
commonMistakes.fix: Prefix public static paths with / so they resolve consistently regardless of route depth.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assigning duplicate id attributes on the same page
commonMistakes.fix: Keep every id globally unique per document so fragment jumps and <label for> bindings never collide.

interviewQA.question: How does /img/hero.jpg differ from img/hero.jpg on /courses/html?
interviewQA.answer: /img/hero.jpg resolves to https://site.com/img/hero.jpg; img/hero.jpg resolves to https://site.com/courses/img/hero.jpg.

interviewQA.question: What subtle side effect does <base href="https://example.com/app/"> have?
interviewQA.answer: It rewrites ALL relative URLs on the page, including anchor fragment links like href="#top", which will navigate to /app/#top instead of staying on the current subpage.

sections.title: Images, Tables & Embedded Content
sections.description: Deliver crisp accessible images, well-structured data tables, and sandboxed iframes.

lessons.title: Accessible Images: alt, width/height & Lazy Loading
lessons.summary: Images require thoughtful alternative text and explicit intrinsic dimensions to prevent Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS).
explanation: Images require thoughtful alternative text and explicit intrinsic dimensions to prevent Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS).

Informative images need concise alt text describing what the image communicates; purely decorative images should use empty alt="" so screen readers skip them rather than reading the filename. Setting width and height lets browsers reserve aspect-ratio space before download.
Use loading="lazy" for below-the-fold images, but keep the above-the-fold hero image eager with fetchpriority="high".

codeExample.title: Zero-CLS Accessible Image Markup

keyPoints: Use descriptive alt text for meaningful images and alt="" for decorative graphics.
Always include width and height attributes to prevent layout shifts while loading.
Never put loading="lazy" on the Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) hero image.

commonMistakes.mistake: Omitting the alt attribute completely on decorative icons
commonMistakes.fix: Use alt="" (empty string) for decorative images; omitting alt causes screen readers to read the raw file URL.

commonMistakes.mistake: Lazy-loading the hero banner at the top of the viewport
commonMistakes.fix: Keep above-the-fold hero images eager so LCP stays fast.

interviewQA.question: What is the difference between alt="" and omitting alt?
interviewQA.answer: alt="" marks the image as decorative so assistive tech ignores it; omitting alt treats it as missing metadata and may announce the file path.

interviewQA.question: How do width and height HTML attributes prevent Cumulative Layout Shift?
interviewQA.answer: Browsers compute the intrinsic aspect ratio immediately from width/height and reserve exact vertical space before the image bytes arrive.

lessons.title: Data Tables: thead, tbody, scope & caption
lessons.summary: HTML tables exist for tabular data—never page layout—and rely on semantic header associations for screen reader cell announcements.
explanation: HTML tables exist for tabular data—never page layout—and rely on semantic header associations for screen reader cell announcements.
Provide a <caption> describing the table, group headers in <thead> and body rows in <tbody>, and set scope="col" or scope="row" on <th> cells so users know which header applies to any cell.
Wrap wide tables in an overflow-x-auto container on mobile screens so they never break viewport width.

codeExample.title: Accessible Tabular Data Markup
codeExample.code:
Course Completion Thresholds
Assessment Pass Mark
Section Quiz 70%

keyPoints: <caption> acts as the accessible title for a <table>.
Use <th scope="col"> for column headers and <th scope="row"> for row headers.
Use <thead>, <tbody>, and <tfoot> to enable sticky headers and print pagination.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using <td> with bold CSS instead of <th> for header rows
commonMistakes.fix: Always use <th> with scope attributes so screen readers announce column context per cell.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using tables for multi-column page layouts
commonMistakes.fix: Use CSS Grid or Flexbox for visual layout; keep <table> strictly for relational data.

interviewQA.question: What does scope="col" on a <th> element do?
interviewQA.answer: It explicitly associates that header cell with all data cells below it in the same column for assistive technologies.

interviewQA.question: How do complex multi-level header tables link cells?
interviewQA.answer: By giving <th> cells unique id attributes and referencing them in each <td> via the headers="id1 id2" attribute.

lessons.title: Native Audio & Video Elements
lessons.summary: HTML5 embeds media natively with <video> and <audio>, supporting multiple codec <source> fallbacks and accessible <track> captions.
explanation: HTML5 embeds media natively with <video> and <audio>, supporting multiple codec <source> fallbacks and accessible <track> captions.
Always provide captions via <track kind="captions" src="...vtt" srclang="en"> and set preload="metadata" to avoid downloading gigabytes of video until the user interacts.
Autoplay in modern browsers only succeeds when muted is also present (<video autoplay muted playsinline>).

codeExample.title: Accessible Multi-Source Video Player
codeExample.code:
<video controls preload="metadata" poster="/media/thumb.jpg" width="720">
  <source src="/media/intro.webm" type="video/webm" />
  <source src="/media/intro.mp4" type="video/mp4" />
  <track kind="captions" src="/media/intro.vtt" srclang="en" label="English" default />
  Your browser does not support embedded video.
</video>

keyPoints: Order <source> elements from most efficient codec (AV1/WebM) to widest fallback (MP4).
Always include <track kind="captions"> using WebVTT (.vtt) for accessibility.
Browsers block unmuted autoplay; include muted and playsinline for ambient background video.

commonMistakes.mistake: Setting autoplay without muted
commonMistakes.fix: Include muted (or avoid autoplay altogether) so browser autoplay policies do not silently fail playback.

commonMistakes.mistake: Omitting the poster attribute on video players
commonMistakes.fix: Provide a crisp poster image and preload="metadata" so the player looks complete before playback.

interviewQA.question: Why do browsers allow <video autoplay muted> but block unmuted autoplay?
interviewQA.answer: Autoplay policies prevent unexpected audio from disrupting users while permitting silent ambient motion.

interviewQA.question: What file format does the HTML <track> element use?
interviewQA.answer: WebVTT (.vtt), a plain-text timestamped subtitle and caption format.

lessons.title: Iframes, Sandboxing & Security Headers
lessons.summary: The <iframe> element embeds external documents in an isolated browsing context, requiring strict security hardening.
explanation: The <iframe> element embeds external documents in an isolated browsing context, requiring strict security hardening.

Always give every <iframe> a descriptive title attribute for screen readers, use loading="lazy", and apply the sandbox attribute with minimal capabilities (e.g., sandbox="allow-scripts") to block top-level navigation and form hijacking.
Never combine allow-scripts and allow-same-origin in sandbox on untrusted third-party embeds, as that lets the embedded script strip its own sandbox.

codeExample.title: Hardened Sandboxed Iframe
codeExample.code:
<iframe
  src="https://sandbox.example.dev/demo"
  title="Interactive CSS Grid Demo"
  width="640"
  height="360"
  loading="lazy"
  sandbox="allow-scripts"
  referrerpolicy="no-referrer"
></iframe>

keyPoints: Every <iframe> requires a descriptive title attribute for WCAG compliance.
An empty sandbox="" applies maximum restrictions; add only minimal allow-* tokens.
Combining allow-scripts + allow-same-origin on untrusted content defeats sandboxing.

commonMistakes.mistake: Embedding untrusted iframes without the sandbox attribute
commonMistakes.fix: Apply sandbox with least-privilege permissions and strict referrerPolicy.

commonMistakes.mistake: Leaving out the title attribute on iframes
commonMistakes.fix: Screen reader users hear "frame" with no context unless title describes the embedded content.

interviewQA.question: Why is sandbox="allow-scripts allow-same-origin" dangerous for untrusted embeds?
interviewQA.answer: If the iframe shares origin and can execute JavaScript, it can access its own frameElement in the parent DOM and remove the sandbox attribute.

interviewQA.question: How does a server prevent its own pages from being clickjacked inside an attacker’s iframe?
interviewQA.answer: By sending Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'none' (or 'self').

sections.title: Forms & Input Controls
sections.description: Design resilient, accessible HTML forms with proper labels, input types, fieldsets, and mobile keyboards.

lessons.title: Form Architecture: action, method, label & name
lessons.summary: Forms collect structured user input and submit key-value pairs determined strictly by each control’s name attribute.
explanation: Forms collect structured user input and submit key-value pairs determined strictly by each control’s name attribute.

Every input must be programmatically associated with a <label> via matching for/id attributes (or wrapping). Without a name attribute, an input’s value is omitted from FormData and HTTP form submission.
Always specify type="button" on non-submit buttons inside a <form>; the default type of <button> inside a form is submit!

codeExample.title: Accessible Form with Explicit Labels
codeExample.code:
<form action="/api/enroll" method="post">
  <label for="email">Work Email</label>
  <input id="email" name="email" type="email" autocomplete="email" required />
  <button type="button" id="cancel-btn">Cancel</button>
  <button type="submit">Enroll</button>
</form>

keyPoints: Only form controls with a name attribute are serialized on submit.
Explicit <label for="id"> increases click target area and informs screen readers.
Default <button> type inside <form> is "submit"—always set type="button" for secondary buttons.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using placeholder instead of <label>
commonMistakes.fix: Placeholders vanish as soon as typing begins and fail WCAG contrast/accessibility; always include a visible <label>.

commonMistakes.mistake: Forgetting type="button" on a Cancel or toggle button inside a form
commonMistakes.fix: Set type="button" explicitly so clicking it does not accidentally submit the form.

interviewQA.question: Why is a control missing from new FormData(form)?
interviewQA.answer: Most commonly because the input lacks a name attribute or is currently disabled (disabled inputs are excluded from submission, unlike readonly inputs).

interviewQA.question: What is the difference between disabled and readonly inputs?
interviewQA.answer: disabled inputs cannot receive focus and are NOT submitted with the form; readonly inputs can be focused/copied and ARE submitted.

lessons.title: Semantic Input Types, inputmode & autocomplete
lessons.summary: Modern HTML input types unlock native pickers, tailored mobile keyboards, and password-manager autofill.
explanation: Modern HTML input types unlock native pickers, tailored mobile keyboards, and password-manager autofill.

Use type="email", type="url", type="date", type="number", and type="search" appropriately. For numeric codes like OTPs or postal codes that should not show increment spinners or strip leading zeros, pair type="text" with inputmode="numeric".
Add standard autocomplete tokens (email, current-password, new-password, one-time-code) to dramatically reduce form friction.

codeExample.title: Mobile-Friendly Inputs with inputmode & autocomplete
codeExample.code:
<label for="otp">6-Digit Verification Code</label>
<input
  id="otp"
  name="otp"
  type="text"
  inputmode="numeric"
  autocomplete="one-time-code"
  pattern="[0-9]{6}"
  maxlength="6"
/>

keyPoints: inputmode="numeric" opens the numeric keypad on mobile without <input type="number"> quirks.
autocomplete="one-time-code" enables automatic SMS code autofill on iOS and Android.
type="number" strips leading zeros and allows "e" for scientific notation.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using type="number" for credit cards, ZIP codes, or OTPs
commonMistakes.fix: Use type="text" with inputmode="numeric" and pattern so leading zeros are preserved and scroll-wheel changes don’t corrupt values.

commonMistakes.mistake: Setting autocomplete="off" on login forms
commonMistakes.fix: Use autocomplete="username" and autocomplete="current-password" so password managers work smoothly.

interviewQA.question: Why is type="text" inputmode="numeric" preferred over type="number" for postal codes?
interviewQA.answer: Postal codes like "02138" have significant leading zeros and are identifiers, not arithmetic quantities; type="number" also changes value on mouse wheel scroll.

interviewQA.question: How does autocomplete="new-password" help users?
interviewQA.answer: It signals password managers to generate and save a strong password instead of autofilling an existing login credential.

lessons.title: Fieldset, Legend, Radios, Checkboxes & Datalist
lessons.summary: Group related controls like radio buttons or shipping fields inside <fieldset> with a <legend> for crystal-clear accessible context.
explanation: Group related controls like radio buttons or shipping fields inside <fieldset> with a <legend> for crystal-clear accessible context.

Radio buttons belong to the same mutually exclusive group when they share the exact same name attribute. For combo-box suggestions without heavy JS libraries, link an <input list="..."> to a <datalist>.
Screen readers announce the <legend> text before reading each radio option inside a <fieldset>, eliminating ambiguity.

codeExample.title: Accessible Radio Group & Datalist Suggestions
codeExample.code:
<fieldset>
  <legend>Experience Level</legend>
  <label><input type="radio" name="level" value="beginner" checked /> Beginner</label>
  <label><input type="radio" name="level" value="advanced" /> Advanced</label>
</fieldset>

<label for="lang">Primary Language</label>
<input id="lang" name="lang" list="languages" />
<datalist id="languages">
  <option value="TypeScript"></option>
  <option value="Python"></option>
  <option value="Rust"></option>
</datalist>

keyPoints: Radio buttons become mutually exclusive strictly by sharing the same name attribute.
<fieldset> + <legend> gives screen readers group-level context for radio and checkbox sets.
<datalist> offers native autocomplete suggestions while still allowing free-form text.

commonMistakes.mistake: Giving each radio button a different name attribute
commonMistakes.fix: Use one shared name for the radio group and distinct value attributes per option.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using a heading <h3> instead of <legend> for a radio group question
commonMistakes.fix: Wrap the group in <fieldset> with <legend> so assistive technology announces the question on focus.

interviewQA.question: How do <select> and <datalist> differ?
interviewQA.answer: <select> restricts users strictly to predefined options, whereas <datalist> provides autocomplete suggestions on an <input> while still permitting arbitrary custom input.

interviewQA.question: Why must radio buttons share a name attribute?
interviewQA.answer: Sharing a name links them into a single form field so selecting one automatically deselects the others and arrow keys cycle through them.

lessons.title: Native Constraint Validation & Error Messaging
lessons.summary: HTML5 ships with built-in declarative validation attributes (required, minlength, pattern, min, max) backed by the JavaScript Constraint Validation API.
explanation: HTML5 ships with built-in declarative validation attributes (required, minlength, pattern, min, max) backed by the JavaScript Constraint Validation API.

When custom styling is needed, set novalidate on <form> and inspect input.validity (e.g., valueMissing, patternMismatch) on submit, then link custom error paragraphs to inputs using aria-invalid="true" and aria-describedby="error-id".
Never rely solely on client-side HTML validation for security—always re-validate on the server.

codeExample.title: Accessible Custom Error Binding
codeExample.code: Use 3+ letters, numbers, or underscores.

keyPoints: Built-in attributes (required, pattern, min, max) expose ValidityState via JS.
Connect custom error text to inputs with aria-describedby and aria-invalid="true".
Client-side validation improves UX; server-side validation enforces security.

commonMistakes.mistake: Showing red border color alone on invalid inputs
commonMistakes.fix: Pair color with explicit error text linked via aria-describedby so color-blind and screen-reader users know what to fix.

commonMistakes.mistake: Disabling the Submit button until the form is valid without explaining why
commonMistakes.fix: Keep Submit clickable and announce or focus the first invalid field with clear guidance.

interviewQA.question: What does adding novalidate to a <form> do?
interviewQA.answer: It suppresses native browser tooltip popups on submit so your application can display consistent accessible error summaries while still reading input.validity via JS.

interviewQA.question: How does aria-describedby improve form error UX?
interviewQA.answer: When a user focuses the invalid input, screen readers read both the label and the associated error message text.

sections.title: Responsive Media & Graphics
sections.description: Serve optimal image resolutions with srcset, picture art direction, inline SVG accessibility, and canvas fundamentals.

lessons.title: Responsive Images with srcset & sizes
lessons.summary: Shipping a 2400px desktop photo to a 390px phone wastes bandwidth and slows LCP; srcset and sizes let the browser choose the ideal file.
explanation: Shipping a 2400px desktop photo to a 390px phone wastes bandwidth and slows LCP; srcset and sizes let the browser choose the ideal file.

Width descriptors (400w, 800w, 1600w) tell the browser each file’s pixel width, while sizes tells the browser how wide the image will render in CSS pixels at each viewport breakpoint—allowing the preload scanner to pick the right asset before CSS finishes parsing.
Always include a standard src fallback for older clients and test DPR scaling in browser DevTools.

codeExample.title: Resolution Switching with srcset and sizes

keyPoints: Use w descriptors + sizes for fluid responsive images; use 1x/2x descriptors only for fixed-width icons.
The browser factors in devicePixelRatio automatically (e.g., 400px slot on 2x screen picks 800w).
sizes must reflect your actual CSS layout width, not the file dimensions.

commonMistakes.mistake: Omitting sizes when using w descriptors in srcset
commonMistakes.fix: Without sizes, browsers assume 100vw, causing oversized downloads on multi-column grids.

commonMistakes.mistake: Mixing 2x density descriptors and 800w width descriptors in the same srcset
commonMistakes.fix: Use either width descriptors OR density descriptors, never both together.

interviewQA.question: Why can the browser select the right srcset image before CSS loads?
interviewQA.answer: Because the sizes attribute gives the HTML preload scanner layout width hints directly in the markup.

interviewQA.question: Which image will a 2x Retina phone at 375px wide pick from 400w, 800w, 1600w with sizes="100vw"?
interviewQA.answer: 375 * 2 = 750 physical pixels, so the browser chooses the 800w candidate.

lessons.title: Art Direction & Modern Formats with <picture>
lessons.summary: The <picture> element lets you serve next-gen formats like AVIF and WebP with JPEG fallbacks, or swap crops per viewport.
explanation: The <picture> element lets you serve next-gen formats like AVIF and WebP with JPEG fallbacks, or swap crops per viewport.

The browser evaluates children in order and selects the first matching media query and supported MIME type. The inner element is still mandatory—it holds alt text, sizing, and renders the chosen source.
Place AVIF first, WebP second, and JPEG on the fallback for maximum compression with 100% browser support.

codeExample.title: AVIF/WebP Progressive Enhancement with <picture>

keyPoints: Browsers pick the first <source> whose type and media attributes both match.
inside is required; styling and alt attributes go on the .
Use <picture> for art direction (portrait mobile crop vs landscape desktop crop).

commonMistakes.mistake: Putting alt or class styles on instead of the nested
commonMistakes.fix: Always place alt, width, height, and styling on the inner element.

commonMistakes.mistake: Listing JPEG <source> before AVIF
commonMistakes.fix: Put the smallest modern format (AVIF, then WebP) first because browsers stop at the first supported <source>.

interviewQA.question: When should you use instead of plain ?
interviewQA.answer: Use <picture> when changing image formats (AVIF/WebP fallback) or changing the visual crop/aspect ratio across breakpoints (art direction).

interviewQA.question: What happens if you omit inside ?
interviewQA.answer: Nothing renders because is only a wrapper providing source candidates to its inner .

lessons.title: Inline SVG, viewBox & Accessible Vector Icons
lessons.summary: Scalable Vector Graphics remain razor-sharp at any DPI and can inherit CSS currentColor when inlined directly in HTML.
explanation: Scalable Vector Graphics remain razor-sharp at any DPI and can inherit CSS currentColor when inlined directly in HTML.

Always define viewBox="0 0 W H" so vectors scale predictably. Decorative icons inside labeled buttons should carry aria-hidden="true"; standalone meaningful SVGs need role="img" and an accessible <title>.
Use fill="currentColor" or stroke="currentColor" so icons adapt effortlessly between light and dark themes.

codeExample.title: Accessible Inline SVG Patterns

keyPoints: viewBox defines the internal coordinate system enabling crisp responsive scaling.
Mark decorative icons aria-hidden="true" to avoid noisy screen reader output.
currentColor binds SVG stroke/fill directly to the parent element’s CSS text color.

commonMistakes.mistake: Leaving out aria-hidden="true" on decorative button icons
commonMistakes.fix: Hide decorative icons from assistive tech and rely on the button’s visible text or aria-label.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using inline SVGs for massive complex photographs
commonMistakes.fix: Keep SVG for icons, logos, and diagrams; use AVIF/WebP/JPEG for photography.

interviewQA.question: How does viewBox differ from width and height on an <svg>?
interviewQA.answer: viewBox sets the internal virtual coordinate grid, while width and height control the rendered CSS box size on screen.

interviewQA.question: How do you make a standalone SVG chart accessible?
interviewQA.answer: Add role="img", aria-labelledby="chart-title", and a child <title id="chart-title"> describing the insight.

lessons.title: HTML5 Canvas vs SVG Decision Guide
lessons.summary: The <canvas> element provides a pixel-based bitmap drawing surface driven by JavaScript 2D or WebGL APIs.
explanation: The <canvas> element provides a pixel-based bitmap drawing surface driven by JavaScript 2D or WebGL APIs.

Unlike SVG—where every shape is a DOM node with event listeners and CSS styling—<canvas> paints directly onto a pixel buffer. Because pixels are opaque to screen readers, provide fallback content between <canvas> and </canvas> or mirror key metrics in accessible HTML.
Scale canvas backing store by window.devicePixelRatio so lines and text stay crisp on Retina screens.

codeExample.title: Accessible Canvas with Fallback Description
codeExample.code: Quiz score trend: 75% in Section 1, 88% in Section 2, 95% in Section 3.

keyPoints: SVG is retained-mode (DOM nodes); Canvas is immediate-mode (pixel bitmap).
Choose Canvas for thousands of animated particles, games, or real-time video effects.
Always provide accessible fallback text or ARIA labels for informational canvases.

commonMistakes.mistake: Resizing a <canvas> with CSS width/height without matching the backing buffer
commonMistakes.fix: Set canvas.width = cssWidth * dpr and scale the 2D context so drawings never look blurry or stretched.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using <canvas> for simple UI icons or static charts
commonMistakes.fix: Prefer SVG for crisp zoomable UI graphics and built-in DOM accessibility.

interviewQA.question: When is <canvas> faster than <svg>?
interviewQA.answer: When rendering thousands of dynamic shapes per frame (games, heatmaps, particle physics), because SVG DOM reconciliation becomes a bottleneck.

interviewQA.question: What is the text placed inside <canvas>...</canvas> used for?
interviewQA.answer: It serves as accessible fallback content for assistive technologies and environments without canvas support.

sections.title: Native Interactive Elements
sections.description: Build zero-dependency disclosures, modals, popovers, and templates using modern standard HTML.

lessons.title: Disclosures & Accordions with <details> and <summary>
lessons.summary: <details> and <summary> create keyboard-accessible expandable sections without a single line of JavaScript.
explanation: <details> and <summary> create keyboard-accessible expandable sections without a single line of JavaScript.
Adding the same name attribute across sibling <details> elements (supported in modern browsers) turns them into an exclusive accordion where opening one automatically closes the others.
Keep <summary> concise and avoid putting headings or interactive links inside <summary> without careful testing.

codeExample.title: Exclusive Native HTML Accordion
codeExample.code:

keyPoints: <summary> is the always-visible interactive disclosure trigger.
Adding the boolean open attribute renders the panel expanded by default.
Matching name attributes create mutually exclusive accordions natively.

commonMistakes.mistake: Building custom <div onclick> accordions without aria-expanded or keyboard handlers
commonMistakes.fix: Use native <details>/<summary> for free keyboard Enter/Space support and accessible semantics.

commonMistakes.mistake: Omitting <summary> inside <details>
commonMistakes.fix: Always provide a clear <summary>; otherwise browsers display a generic "Details" label.

interviewQA.question: What event fires when a <details> element opens or closes?
interviewQA.answer: The toggle event fires on the <details> element, where event.target.open reflects the new boolean state.

interviewQA.question: How do you make native <details> elements behave as a single-open accordion?
interviewQA.answer: Assign the exact same name attribute to each <details> in the group.

lessons.title: Native Modals with <dialog>
lessons.summary: The HTML <dialog> element renders accessible modals on the browser top layer—above every z-index stacking context.
explanation: The HTML <dialog> element renders accessible modals on the browser top layer—above every z-index stacking context.

Calling dialog.showModal() activates the ::backdrop pseudo-element, traps keyboard focus inside the modal, enables Escape-to-close automatically, and makes background content inert. Using <form method="dialog"> closes the dialog and sets dialog.returnValue automatically.
Prefer dialog.showModal() for blocking confirmations and dialog.show() for non-modal floating panels.

codeExample.title: Native Modal with form method="dialog"
codeExample.code:
Reset Progress?

This clears all local quiz scores.

keyPoints: showModal() places the dialog in the top layer, defeating z-index bugs permanently.
Escape key automatically fires the cancel and close events on modal dialogs.
<form method="dialog"> closes the dialog on submit and stores the clicked button value in dialog.returnValue.

commonMistakes.mistake: Toggling <dialog open> via attribute instead of calling showModal()
commonMistakes.fix: Setting the open attribute creates a non-modal dialog with NO backdrop and NO focus trap; use showModal() for true modals.

commonMistakes.mistake: Fighting z-index: 999999 on custom modal overlays
commonMistakes.fix: Native <dialog> via showModal() lives in the browser Top Layer above all page z-indexes.

interviewQA.question: What is the difference between dialog.show() and dialog.showModal()?
interviewQA.answer: show() opens a non-modal dialog where the rest of the page stays interactive; showModal() renders on the top layer with ::backdrop, Esc-to-close, and inert background.

interviewQA.question: What does <form method="dialog"> do when submitted?
interviewQA.answer: It closes the ancestor <dialog> without making a network request and sets dialog.returnValue to the submit button’s value.

lessons.title: The Native Popover API
lessons.summary: The HTML Popover API (popover attribute + popovertarget) creates light-dismiss tooltips, menus, and dropdowns natively in the top layer.
explanation: The HTML Popover API (popover attribute + popovertarget) creates light-dismiss tooltips, menus, and dropdowns natively in the top layer.
With popover="auto" (or bare popover), clicking outside or pressing Escape automatically dismisses the popover and closes other auto popovers—zero event-listener cleanup required.
Use popover="manual" only for persistent notifications or toasts that should not close when the user clicks elsewhere.

codeExample.title: Declarative Zero-JS Popover Menu
codeExample.code: HTML CSS

keyPoints: popover renders in the top layer without clipping inside overflow: hidden containers.
popover="auto" provides automatic light-dismiss (outside click + Escape).
popovertarget links a <button> to a popover element’s id declaratively.

commonMistakes.mistake: Confusing <dialog> showModal() with popover
commonMistakes.fix: Use showModal() when the background must become inert; use popover for non-blocking dropdowns, menus, and tooltips.

commonMistakes.mistake: Forgetting that popovers are display: none until opened
commonMistakes.fix: Style the open state with the :popover-open CSS pseudo-class.

interviewQA.question: How does popover="auto" differ from popover="manual"?
interviewQA.answer: auto popovers light-dismiss on outside clicks/Escape and auto-close sibling auto popovers; manual popovers must be closed explicitly.

interviewQA.question: Why does the Popover API eliminate overflow: hidden clipping bugs?
interviewQA.answer: Because open popovers are promoted to the browser’s top layer outside normal ancestor stacking and clipping contexts.

lessons.title: HTML <template>, <slot> & inert Attribute
lessons.summary: <template> holds inert DOM fragments for client-side cloning, while the global inert attribute disables entire subtrees from focus, clicks, and screen readers.
explanation: <template> holds inert DOM fragments for client-side cloning, while the global inert attribute disables entire subtrees from focus, clicks, and screen readers.

Markup inside <template> is parsed into a DocumentFragment without loading images or running scripts until cloned with template.content.cloneNode(true). Meanwhile, inert is the cleanest way to disable background regions behind drawers.
Use document.importNode(tpl.content, true) or tpl.content.cloneNode(true) when stamping repeated DOM rows.

codeExample.title: Inert Template Cloning

keyPoints: Content inside <template> does not render and does not fetch images until cloned into the live DOM.
The global inert boolean attribute removes all descendants from tab order, pointer events, and the accessibility tree.
<slot> projects light-DOM children inside Shadow DOM Web Components.

commonMistakes.mistake: Querying elements directly inside <template> via tpl.querySelector()
commonMistakes.fix: Always query tpl.content.querySelector(...) because template children live on its DocumentFragment .content property.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using pointer-events: none alone to disable a drawer background
commonMistakes.fix: Use the inert attribute so keyboard Tab navigation and screen readers are also properly blocked.

interviewQA.question: Why don’t tags inside
interviewQA.answer: The HTML parser places template contents in an inert DocumentFragment belonging to an inactive document until cloned into the active DOM.

interviewQA.question: What three interactions does the global inert attribute disable?
interviewQA.answer: Pointer/click events, keyboard focus/tabbing, and exposure to assistive technologies (accessibility tree).

sections.title: Metadata, Open Graph & Structured Data
sections.description: Optimize pages for search indexing, rich link previews, canonical URLs, and international audiences.

lessons.title: SEO Fundamentals: Canonical, Robots & Meta Descriptions
lessons.summary: Clean HTML metadata prevents duplicate-content indexing penalties and guides search crawlers accurately.
explanation: Clean HTML metadata prevents duplicate-content indexing penalties and guides search crawlers accurately.
Whenever query strings (?ref=nav or ?sort=asc) generate duplicate URLs for the same page, <link rel="canonical"> tells search engines which single authoritative URL should accumulate ranking signals.
Keep <title> around 50–60 characters and <meta name="description"> concise (140–160 characters) with genuine page specifics.

codeExample.title: Canonical & Crawler Directives
codeExample.code:
<head>
  <title>PostgreSQL Course — IT Courses</title>
  <meta name="description" content="Master PostgreSQL indexing, MVCC, window functions, and query tuning across 48 lessons." />
  <link rel="canonical" href="https://itcourses.dev/courses/postgresql" />
  <meta name="robots" content="index, follow" />
</head>

keyPoints: rel="canonical" consolidates SEO signals when multiple URLs serve identical content.
Use noindex on private dashboards or temporary staging previews.
Every route should dynamically update its <title> and canonical link.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using relative URLs inside <link rel="canonical">
commonMistakes.fix: Always provide a full absolute URL including https:// and domain in canonical links.

commonMistakes.mistake: Accidentally leaving noindex on production marketing pages
commonMistakes.fix: Audit <meta name="robots"> before production launches so search engines can crawl public routes.

interviewQA.question: Why is <link rel="canonical"> important on paginated or filtered catalog pages?
interviewQA.answer: It prevents query parameter variants like ?utm_source=twitter from splitting search authority across duplicate URLs.

interviewQA.question: Does <meta name="keywords"> still influence Google search rankings?
interviewQA.answer: No, modern search engines ignore meta keywords due to historical spam; focus on semantic headings, content quality, and structured data.

lessons.title: Open Graph & Twitter/X Social Share Cards
lessons.summary: Open Graph (og:*) and Twitter Card meta tags control the title, summary, and preview image rendered when links are shared in chat apps and feeds.
explanation: Open Graph (og:*) and Twitter Card meta tags control the title, summary, and preview image rendered when links are shared in chat apps and feeds.
Always provide an absolute HTTPS URL for og:image with a 1.91:1 landscape aspect ratio (1200×630) and pair it with og:image:alt for accessibility.
Include twitter:card="summary_large_image" so platforms display a prominent preview banner rather than a tiny thumbnail.

codeExample.title: Complete Social Share Meta Block
codeExample.code:
<meta property="og:type" content="website" />
<meta property="og:title" content="IT Courses — 23 Programming Tracks" />
<meta property="og:description" content="Learn languages, databases, and interview DSA with verifiable certificates." />
<meta property="og:image" content="https://itcourses.dev/og-card.png" />
<meta property="og:image:alt" content="IT Courses curriculum overview" />
<meta name="twitter:card" content="summary_large_image" />

keyPoints: Open Graph uses property="og:*" while standard meta and Twitter tags use name="...".
og:image must be an absolute URL—social scrapers do not execute client-side JS.
Standard recommended dimensions for og:image are 1200×630 pixels.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using a relative path like content="/og.png" in og:image
commonMistakes.fix: Social link scrapers require full absolute https:// URLs to fetch preview images reliably.

commonMistakes.mistake: Injecting Open Graph tags only via client-side React useEffect
commonMistakes.fix: Social bots generally read raw initial HTML; emit OG tags in static HTML or SSR responses.

interviewQA.question: Why do Open Graph tags use property instead of name?
interviewQA.answer: Open Graph is based on RDFa, which specifies the property attribute for predicate URIs like og:title.

interviewQA.question: Why might social previews fail on a client-rendered SPA?
interviewQA.answer: Most social crawlers do not execute JavaScript, so dynamic route-specific OG tags must be server-rendered or prerendered.

lessons.title: JSON-LD Structured Data (Schema.org)
lessons.summary: Embedding <script type="application/ld+json"> supplies explicit Schema.org entities (Course, FAQPage, Organization) directly to search engines.
explanation: Embedding <script type="application/ld+json"> supplies explicit Schema.org entities (Course, FAQPage, Organization) directly to search engines.
JSON-LD is preferred over inline Microdata attributes because it stays cleanly decoupled from HTML layout markup and is easy to validate and maintain.
Ensure every claim in JSON-LD (course title, provider, pricing) matches visible text on the page to avoid manual search penalties.

codeExample.title: Schema.org Course JSON-LD Block
codeExample.code:
<script type="application/ld+json">
{
  "@context": "https://schema.org",
  "@type": "Course",
  "name": "Python Engineering Track",
  "description": "Beginner to Advanced Python with 48 lessons and exams.",
  "provider": {
    "@type": "Organization",
    "name": "IT Courses"
  }
}
</script>

keyPoints: Browsers do not execute scripts with type="application/ld+json"; they treat them as data blocks.
JSON-LD enables rich search results (course cards, ratings, breadcrumbs, FAQs).
Structured data must accurately reflect visible on-page content.

commonMistakes.mistake: Leaving trailing commas inside JSON-LD blocks
commonMistakes.fix: JSON-LD must be strictly valid JSON—no comments and no trailing commas.

commonMistakes.mistake: Marking up hidden content that users cannot see on the page
commonMistakes.fix: Only include structured data describing visible content on that URL.

interviewQA.question: Why is JSON-LD preferred over Microdata (itemscope/itemprop)?
interviewQA.answer: JSON-LD separates structured metadata from presentation DOM, preventing layout refactors from breaking schema markup.

interviewQA.question: Does the browser run JavaScript inside <script type="application/ld+json">?
interviewQA.answer: No; any non-JavaScript MIME type causes the browser to skip script execution and simply preserve the text data block.

lessons.title: Internationalization: lang, dir & hreflang
lessons.summary: Global web apps declare script direction (dir="ltr" or dir="rtl"), inline language shifts, and localized alternate URLs via hreflang.
explanation: Global web apps declare script direction (dir="ltr" or dir="rtl"), inline language shifts, and localized alternate URLs via hreflang.

When quoting a phrase in another language inside an English paragraph, mark the span with lang="fr" or lang="ja". Use <bdi> (Bidirectional Isolate) around user-generated usernames so right-to-left characters never scramble surrounding punctuation.
Include rel="alternate" hreflang="x-default" alongside localized versions so search engines serve the right regional page.

codeExample.title: Multilingual Markup & Bidirectional Isolation
codeExample.code: Top scorer: أحمد — 98% (Félicitations)

keyPoints: dir="rtl" on <html> flips document layout and reading direction for Arabic and Hebrew.
<bdi> isolates unknown-direction user text so adjacent numbers and punctuation stay intact.
hreflang links must be reciprocal across language variants.

commonMistakes.mistake: Interpolating arbitrary user names next to numbers without <bdi>
commonMistakes.fix: Wrap user-supplied strings in <bdi> to prevent Unicode bidirectional algorithm scrambling.

commonMistakes.mistake: Forgetting lang attributes on inline foreign-language phrases
commonMistakes.fix: Add lang="es" (etc.) on inline elements so screen readers switch pronunciation engines smoothly.

interviewQA.question: What problem does the <bdi> element solve?
interviewQA.answer: It isolates bidirectional text (such as an Arabic username inside an English sentence) so the Unicode BiDi algorithm doesn’t reorder neighboring punctuation or numbers.

interviewQA.question: What does hreflang="x-default" designate?
interviewQA.answer: The fallback page URL for users whose language/region does not match any explicitly listed hreflang variant.

sections.title: WAI-ARIA & Accessibility Engineering
sections.description: Apply the First Rule of ARIA, live regions, keyboard roving tabindex, and accessible custom widgets.

lessons.title: The First Rule of ARIA & Accessibility Tree
lessons.summary: Every browser builds an Accessibility Tree from the DOM—and native HTML elements already carry built-in roles, states, and keyboard behaviors.
explanation: Every browser builds an Accessibility Tree from the DOM—and native HTML elements already carry built-in roles, states, and keyboard behaviors.

The First Rule of ARIA states: if you can use a native HTML element (<button>, <a href>, <input>) with the semantics you need, do so instead of repurposing a <div> with ARIA. Remember: ARIA only changes what assistive technology announces—it NEVER adds keyboard listeners.
Test every interactive screen using only Tab, Shift+Tab, Enter, Space, and Arrow keys.

codeExample.title: Native Button vs Incomplete ARIA Div
codeExample.code: ...

keyPoints: Native HTML beats ARIA-patched divs because native elements include keyboard and focus behavior.
ARIA attributes modify the Accessibility Tree only—never visual styling or JS events.
aria-expanded + aria-controls communicate disclosure state cleanly.

commonMistakes.mistake: Adding role="button" to a <div> without tabindex="0" and Enter/Space keydown handlers
commonMistakes.fix: Use a real <button type="button"> instead.

commonMistakes.mistake: Putting role="presentation" on a focusable element
commonMistakes.fix: Never hide focusable elements from the accessibility tree; screen reader users will land on silent phantom stops.

interviewQA.question: What is the First Rule of ARIA?
interviewQA.answer: Do not use ARIA if a native HTML element or attribute already provides the semantics and behavior you need.

interviewQA.question: What happens if you put aria-hidden="true" on a focusable button?
interviewQA.answer: Keyboard users can still Tab to it, creating a confusing "ghost" focus stop that screen readers cannot announce—a WCAG violation.

lessons.title: ARIA Live Regions & Dynamic Status Announcements
lessons.summary: Single-page applications update content without full reloads, so screen readers rely on ARIA live regions to announce toasts, quiz feedback, and search result counts.
explanation: Single-page applications update content without full reloads, so screen readers rely on ARIA live regions to announce toasts, quiz feedback, and search result counts.

Use aria-live="polite" (or role="status") for non-urgent updates like "Showing 12 courses" or "Code copied", and aria-live="assertive" (or role="alert") strictly for urgent errors like failed form validation.
Render the live region container in the DOM BEFORE injecting text into it; inserting a brand-new element with aria-live simultaneously can be missed by some screen readers.

codeExample.title: Polite Status vs Assertive Alert Live Regions
codeExample.code:
Quiz saved: 7 of 8 correct.
Please enter a valid email address.

keyPoints: role="status" implies aria-live="polite"; role="alert" implies aria-live="assertive".
aria-atomic="true" announces the entire region text rather than just the changed text node.
Keep live region containers mounted before updating their inner text.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using aria-live="assertive" for routine notifications or counters
commonMistakes.fix: Reserve assertive/alert for urgent errors; use polite/status for normal updates so you do not interrupt ongoing speech.

commonMistakes.mistake: Mounting and unmounting the aria-live wrapper at the exact moment text changes
commonMistakes.fix: Keep the live region node persistent in the layout and update its children.

interviewQA.question: When should you choose aria-live="polite" over aria-live="assertive"?
interviewQA.answer: Use polite for non-critical feedback (toast confirmations, filter counts) so the screen reader finishes its current sentence; use assertive only for critical errors or warnings.

interviewQA.question: What does aria-atomic="true" control?
interviewQA.answer: It instructs assistive tech to read the whole live region as one coherent unit when any part of it changes.

lessons.title: Focus Management, tabindex & Roving Tabindex
lessons.summary: Predictable focus order lets keyboard users navigate complex UIs like tabs, toolbars, and drawers effortlessly.
explanation: Predictable focus order lets keyboard users navigate complex UIs like tabs, toolbars, and drawers effortlessly.

Never use positive tabindex values (tabindex="1", "2") because they hijack natural DOM reading order. Use tabindex="0" to include a custom widget in natural order, and tabindex="-1" to make headings or panels programmatically focusable via element.focus().
For composite widgets like tab lists, apply roving tabindex: active tab has tabindex="0", inactive tabs have tabindex="-1", and Left/Right arrow keys move focus between them.

codeExample.title: Accessible Tablist with Roving Tabindex

keyPoints: tabindex="0" inserts an element into natural DOM tab order; tabindex="-1" allows JS .focus() only.
Avoid positive tabindex (>0)—fix DOM source order instead.
Roving tabindex keeps Tab presses fast across multi-item toolbars and tab lists.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using tabindex="1", tabindex="2" to patch visual CSS reordering
commonMistakes.fix: Keep DOM order matching visual order and avoid positive tabindex values completely.

commonMistakes.mistake: Removing focus outlines with outline: none
commonMistakes.fix: Style crisp :focus-visible rings so keyboard users always see where focus is located.

interviewQA.question: What is the difference between tabindex="0" and tabindex="-1"?
interviewQA.answer: tabindex="0" makes an element reachable by pressing Tab in natural DOM order; tabindex="-1" excludes it from Tab order while still allowing JavaScript element.focus().

interviewQA.question: Why is :focus-visible better than :focus for styling outlines?
interviewQA.answer: :focus-visible displays the focus ring for keyboard navigation while avoiding distracting outlines on mouse clicks for buttons.

lessons.title: Accessible Name Computation: aria-label vs aria-labelledby
lessons.summary: Assistive technologies compute an element’s accessible name using a strict precedence algorithm.
explanation: Assistive technologies compute an element’s accessible name using a strict precedence algorithm.

aria-labelledby takes highest priority (even overriding visible text and aria-label), followed by aria-label, then native host-language labels (<label for>, alt, visible button text), and finally title as a last resort.
Prefer aria-labelledby pointing to visible headings over hidden aria-label strings so labels automatically stay translated and synchronized.

codeExample.title: Accessible Name Precedence Examples
codeExample.code: Section 1 Quiz

keyPoints: Accessible name precedence: aria-labelledby > aria-label > native label/text > title.
Icon-only buttons MUST have an aria-label or sr-only text.
aria-labelledby can combine multiple IDs (aria-labelledby="item-name delete-verb").

commonMistakes.mistake: Putting aria-label="Edit" on a button whose visible text is "Save Changes"
commonMistakes.fix: aria-label overrides visible text for screen readers and breaks voice-control commands ("Click Save Changes"); ensure accessible names start with visible label text.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using title attributes as the sole label on icon buttons
commonMistakes.fix: title tooltips are inaccessible on touch devices and unreliable across screen readers; use aria-label.

interviewQA.question: What happens if a button has both visible text "Submit" and aria-label="Send Exam"?
interviewQA.answer: Screen readers announce "Send Exam" because aria-label takes precedence over inner text—which violates WCAG Label in Name unless the visible text is included.

interviewQA.question: Why can aria-labelledby reference a hidden element?
interviewQA.answer: The Accessible Name spec explicitly resolves IDs referenced by aria-labelledby even if the target element has hidden or display: none.

sections.title: Web Components & Shadow DOM
sections.description: Author reusable framework-agnostic Custom Elements with Shadow DOM encapsulation and declarative slots.

lessons.title: Custom Elements Lifecycle & Naming Rules
lessons.summary: Web Components let you define native HTML tags with custom behavior backed by standard browser APIs.
explanation: Web Components let you define native HTML tags with custom behavior backed by standard browser APIs.

Every custom element tag name MUST contain a hyphen (e.g., <course-badge>) so it never collides with future built-in HTML tags. Lifecycle callbacks—connectedCallback, disconnectedCallback, and attributeChangedCallback—manage setup, cleanup, and reactive attributes.
Clean up event listeners and timers in disconnectedCallback to prevent memory leaks in single-page apps.

codeExample.title: Custom Element Tag Usage & Definition
codeExample.code:
<course-badge level="Advanced" score="95"></course-badge>
<script type="module">
  class CourseBadge extends HTMLElement {
    connectedCallback() {
      this.textContent = `${this.getAttribute('level')} (${this.getAttribute('score')}%)`;
    }
  }
  customElements.define('course-badge', CourseBadge);
</script>

keyPoints: Custom element names must be lowercase and include at least one hyphen (-).
Never read attributes or append children inside constructor(); use connectedCallback().
Observe specific attributes via static observedAttributes = ["score"].

commonMistakes.mistake: Naming a custom element <badge> without a hyphen
commonMistakes.fix: Always include a hyphen such as <it-badge> or customElements.define() throws a SyntaxError.

commonMistakes.mistake: Mutating DOM children inside the constructor()
commonMistakes.fix: Wait until connectedCallback() so the parser has finished constructing the element.

interviewQA.question: Why must Custom Element names contain a hyphen?
interviewQA.answer: The HTML specification guarantees built-in standard tags will never contain a hyphen, permanently preventing name collisions.

interviewQA.question: Which lifecycle callback fires when an observed attribute changes?
interviewQA.answer: attributeChangedCallback(name, oldValue, newValue) fires only for attributes listed in static observedAttributes.

lessons.title: Shadow DOM Encapsulation & Declarative Shadow DOM
lessons.summary: Shadow DOM scopes component CSS and internal markup so global styles cannot leak in and component styles cannot leak out.
explanation: Shadow DOM scopes component CSS and internal markup so global styles cannot leak in and component styles cannot leak out.
Modern browsers also support Declarative Shadow DOM (<template shadowrootmode="open">), allowing server-rendered HTML to attach a Shadow Root during initial HTML parsing with zero JavaScript flash.
Expose deliberate styling hooks via CSS custom properties (--accent) and ::part() rather than breaking encapsulation.

codeExample.title: Declarative Shadow DOM in Pure HTML
codeExample.code: Passed with 92%
codeExample.output: Passed with 92% (scoped styling immediately during HTML parse)

keyPoints: Declarative Shadow DOM renders scoped components before any JavaScript executes.
CSS custom properties (variables) inherit across Shadow DOM boundaries intentionally.
part="name" allows external CSS to style specific internal elements via ::part(name).

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming CSS variables cannot cross Shadow DOM
commonMistakes.fix: Inherited properties (color, font-family) and CSS custom properties DO cross Shadow boundaries; regular selectors do not.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using shadowrootmode="closed" unnecessarily
commonMistakes.fix: Prefer mode="open" so testing tools, analytics, and accessibility audits can inspect the component cleanly.

interviewQA.question: What problem does Declarative Shadow DOM solve?
interviewQA.answer: It enables SSR (Server-Side Rendering) of Web Components without waiting for JavaScript to hydrate and call attachShadow().

interviewQA.question: How can page CSS style a specific element inside an open Shadow Root?
interviewQA.answer: Through inherited CSS custom properties (--var) or by targeting exposed parts with host::part(button).

lessons.title: Content Projection with Named & Default <slot>s
lessons.summary: Slots compose user-supplied light DOM children inside a Shadow DOM layout template while keeping them accessible and SEO-indexable.
explanation: Slots compose user-supplied light DOM children inside a Shadow DOM layout template while keeping them accessible and SEO-indexable.

An unnamed <slot></slot> captures default children, while <slot name="footer"></slot> captures light-DOM elements carrying slot="footer". Fallback content placed inside <slot>Default</slot> renders whenever nothing is projected.
Remember that slotted elements remain in the light DOM and are styled by the host page’s stylesheet (or via ::slotted() in Shadow CSS).
